## Lithosphere and Plate Motion
The lithosphere is a mosaic of rigid plates floating on the ductile asthenosphere. They move due to mantle convection, slab pull, and ridge push, with relative motion measured in centimetres per year (cm yr⁻¹).
Earthquakes are not randomly distributed; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. At divergent boundaries, plates pull apart, causing normal-fault earthquakes at shallow depths. At convergent boundaries, plates collide, producing thrust-fault earthquakes from deep to shallow. At transform boundaries, plates slide past, generating strike-slip earthquakes at shallow to intermediate depths.
Earthquakes cluster at boundaries because plate edges are locked by friction, so strain builds until it exceeds rock strength. Other factors include pre-existing faults concentrating slip, cold brittle lithosphere bordering warm ductile mantle, and curved plate margins forcing localized shear zones.

## Why Earthquakes Cluster at Boundaries
Earthquakes are not randomly scattered; they trace the kinematic framework of plate interactions. They cluster at plate boundaries because of four main reasons: stress accumulation, fault geometry, rheological contrast, and geometric incompatibility.
Stress accumulation happens when plate edges are locked by friction; strain builds until it exceeds rock strength, causing an earthquake. Fault geometry means pre-existing faults concentrate slip. Rheological contrast occurs because cold, brittle lithosphere borders warm, ductile mantle, focusing deformation. Geometric incompatibility arises from curved plate margins forcing localized shear zones.

## Plate Speed and Earthquake Frequency
The Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm per year relative to the North American Plate, while the Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America at about 8 cm per year. These faster plate speeds help explain why large earthquakes happen so often along the Ring of Fire.
Earthquakes occur at different depths: shallow ones (≤10 km) are common at divergent ridges and transform faults, while intermediate to deep ones (30–300 km) happen in the Wadati-Benioff zone of subducting slabs. A typical subduction earthquake at 30 km depth releases energy from both crustal bending and slab dehydration.
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has four stages: interseismic (strain accumulates over decades to centuries), coseismic (sudden slip releases energy in seconds to minutes), postseismic (afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation redistribute stress over months to years), and preseismic (possible precursory signals like foreshocks or slow slip).
Seismic gap theory says that segments that have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. GPS and InSAR monitor plate-scale velocities in cm/yr to refine coupling models.
Key: Seismic gap theory: Segments that have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events.

The coseismic phase is the sudden slip that releases stored elastic energy in seconds to minutes. ## Seismic Gap Theory and Monitoring
The seismic cycle at a convergent margin has four phases: interseismic (strain accumulates in a locked zone over decades to centuries), coseismic (sudden slip releases stored elastic energy in seconds to minutes), postseismic (afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation redistribute stress over months to years), and preseismic (possible precursory signals like foreshocks or slow slip).
Seismic gap theory says that segments of a fault that have not ruptured in a full cycle are candidates for future large events. This helps identify where earthquakes might happen.
GPS and InSAR measure plate-scale velocities in centimeters per year, which helps refine models of how faults are coupled (locked or slipping).
